analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from signing no-poaching agreements that block workers from being hired by competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with one cosponsor, sent to the Senate labor committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: No-poaching agreements are pacts between companies, often between a franchise brand and its franchisees, promising not to solicit or hire each other's employees. This bill would make such agreements unlawful, letting workers sue for actual damages plus punitive damages and attorney's fees, and letting the Federal Trade Commission enforce the ban. It was referred to the Senate labor committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially in industries like fast food, retail, and healthcare where no-poach agreements are common, who would gain the freedom to move to a better-paying employer without a contract standing in the way. Employees harmed by a violation could recover actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees, and the FTC could pursue violators as an unfair method of competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at companies with no-poach pacts

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for two or more employers, including through franchise or contractor agreements, to enter into, enforce, or threaten to enforce any agreement that restricts one from soliciting or hiring the other's employees.
Workers harmed by a violation can sue in federal court for actual damages, punitive damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees.
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban with the same powers it has under the Federal Trade Commission Act.
The bill covers not just fast-food franchising but also contractor-subcontractor arrangements, where no-poach terms are common.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on no-poach agreements, particularly franchise brands and their franchisees, staffing intermediaries, and other companies that use such pacts to hold down turnover and recruiting competition. They would face litigation risk from employees and FTC enforcement, and would have to rewrite franchise and contracting agreements that currently contain hiring restrictions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Franchise brands and employers using no-poach pacts

drawbacks.text: The private right of action allows punitive damages and attorney's fees against employers, which businesses would bear as new litigation cost and risk even for agreements they signed before the ban.

Franchise brands argue that hiring restrictions across a franchise system serve legitimate purposes, such as protecting training investments, and the bill would sweep those arrangements into an antitrust-style prohibition with no exception for them.
The enforcement burden falls on individual workers and courts: recovering damages requires proving actual harm, which can be hard to document when a worker simply is not called back for a job.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers the gains are straightforward: freer movement between employers typically means higher wages and better job matches in the industries where no-poach pacts are concentrated. The costs fall on employers in the form of litigation exposure and loss of a tool for keeping workers in place; an honest supporter would acknowledge the punitive-damages provision is aggressive and that franchise-specific concerns about training investments go unaddressed. On balance the bill is a targeted, enforceable fix to a practice that limits workers' wages and mobility.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the End Employer Collusion Act in the Senate on July 26, 2023, joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren as an original cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill attracted one cosponsor, and the committee took no further action on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use no-poach agreements, especially franchise chains, keep a tool that suppresses worker mobility and wage competition, because the ban never received a hearing or a vote.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action, never holding a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only support came from two Democratic senators, and no member is recorded as opposing it.

industries.note: No-poach terms in franchise agreements are widespread in fast food and retail, and the bill would make them unlawful, exposing franchisors and franchisees to lawsuits and FTC penalties. Workers in these chains stand to gain wage mobility.
The bill covers contractor-subcontractor agreements, a common vehicle for no-poach terms in building services, janitorial work, and healthcare staffing, ending their use of hiring restrictions.
